extracted.intended_audience: improvisation students and teachers; theatre practitioners (beginners through experienced)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for learning, teaching, and performing improvisation with emphasis on storytelling, spontaneity, classroom/workshop techniques, and managing learner anxiety. Useful as a workshop manual for teachers, students, and improvisation companies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the audience aware of risk
rubrics_metrics.description: The best improvisers constantly make you aware of the risk they are taking, even if they don’t call attention to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watching performers tell the story and sense the risk is as important as the story itself; formats should preserve or foreground that risk to retain the thrill of improvisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect formats that foreground improvisational risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Some formats should shove improvisation’s risk into the foreground, others let it linger in the distance, but it must not be forgotten.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a variety of formats so improvisation does not become merely a poor cousin of stand-up or scripted theatre; deliberately choose formats that highlight live risk when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn by doing (take classes / perform live)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you want to learn to improvise, go and take some improv classes — working with others, without a script, in front of an audience teaches far more than passively reading a book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even imperfect classes teach practical skills; treat the book as a supplement or manual for what would happen in a workshop rather than a replacement for practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teachers should be open-minded and focused on student improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers should have an open mind, a genuine desire to see students improve, and adapt exercises into a syllabus tailored to students’ needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t confine exercises to a classroom—this material is meant to be staged; read widely (e.g., Keith Johnstone) and be prepared to adapt and evolve your teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher responsibility for student progress (including refunds)
rubrics_metrics.description: If students are not getting better, it is the teacher’s job to find a way to reach them; if the teacher cannot, be prepared to offer a refund.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid blaming students as 'talentless'; actively diagnose weaknesses by exposing students to failure and providing targeted instruction; take responsibility for outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize lots of turns and high failure-rate learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Students’ primary mission in a workshop is to have lots of turns; teachers should expect and even hope for a high level of failure as part of learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent practice opportunities let teachers diagnose and correct weaknesses; encourage 'we suck and we love to fail!' mindset to reduce anxiety and accelerate learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a supportive, positive classroom culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Learners should be positive, open and contribute to a supportive environment; teachers should foster that atmosphere rather than students carrying the burden of learning alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage students to be interested in others' work, avoid 'prove-yourself' validation-seeking, and emphasize collaboration and mutual support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize storytelling as central to improvisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Storytelling is a big feature of the authors' conception of improvisation; audiences naturally invent stories and expect narrative cause-and-effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use story elements to make improvised material memorable; even when using set-pieces or spectacle, maintain or return to narrative to satisfy audience curiosity about 'what will happen next?'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage comedy to enhance narrative and group bonding
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy can enhance the narrative and serves as a social signal (group bonding) distinct from the triggers of everyday laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use procedures that make audiences laugh from pleasure and combine those with storytelling to amplify impact; recognize laughter’s social function in performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop spontaneity: get out of your head and abandon control
rubrics_metrics.description: First steps in learning to improvise include getting 'out of your head' and abandoning control of the future; move away from seeking 'Right Answers' toward generative play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shift mental mode from trying to retrieve correct responses to embracing options and uncertain outcomes; use exercises that force spontaneous responding rather than deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simple games to train specific cognitive skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Pointing-and-naming games (e.g., say what you point at, say what you last pointed at, say what it is not) test and train short-term memory, creativity, and fluency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Progress through these games to isolate different faculties (memory vs. uninhibited creation); observe group volume and activity as feedback on progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize fluency (pace and minimal gaps) over 'clever' answers
rubrics_metrics.description: In spontaneity exercises the instructor cares about fluency — playing with the same pace and short gaps as easy tasks — rather than finding the most clever or impressive word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure success by reducing silence/gaps and maintaining consistent tempo; avoid self-censoring for cleverness at the expense of flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppress internal censor by adopting joyful, bold delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Playing loudly, brightly and boldly with an attitude of delight silences the internal censor and increases ease and success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate exaggerated positive energy to set the bar and give permission; pronounce even repeated or heard words with joy to reduce inhibition and increase volume and confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy and confidence increase the chance of success
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempting performance with energy, focus and enthusiasm dramatically increases your chances of success compared with timid delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage students to advertise success boldly (big grin, loud voice) even if it risks a larger advertising/delivery gap — the potential payoff is higher than 'safe' under-advertising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'trying your hardest' as a default strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Trying your hardest piles anxiety on and is often counterproductive; instead adopt mild curiosity and let words emerge without over-monitoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the brain less like a retrieval mechanism and more like a 'lucky dip'; use simple prompts (a letter or sound) if you feel stuck rather than intense conscious effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice brief, regular exercises to improve
rubrics_metrics.description: Even people who struggle can get quite good after practicing just five minutes a day for a week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend short daily practice sessions; practice alone if needed or invite others to play to build consistent fluency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize adult vs child learning differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Children want lots of turns and accept imperfection; adults often seek a single perfect turn and fear showing weakness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers should structure opportunities to mimic children's turn-taking (many low-stakes turns) to counteract adults' performance anxiety and learned fear from education systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose students to imperfect work so teachers can diagnose weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: If teachers only see students' best efforts they cannot diagnose problems; seeing failures gives diagnostic opportunities to fix weaknesses before public performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage regular low-stakes, imperfect attempts in-class; normalize failure so teachers can observe and correct recurring issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on craft and process rather than novelty of games
rubrics_metrics.description: The emphasis should be on what games teach improvisers about performance (craft and process) rather than on learning a wide variety of novelty 'hoop' games.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select exercises for their transferable lessons about performing for an audience rather than for mere novelty; prefer depth over breadth when curating exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use teacher demonstration to set permissive norms
rubrics_metrics.description: A teacher demonstrating exaggerated loudness/energy optionally parodies timid responses then models the desired bold style to raise the group's permission to play big.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contrasts (whisper vs. bellow, timid vs. delighted) to show students what is expected and to reduce their fear of standing out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical techniques to regain production when stuck
rubrics_metrics.description: If you feel your 'word well' has run dry, start with a sound or a letter (e.g., 'Pr...') until a word or phrase emerges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mechanical prompts to restart fluency rather than freezing; then immediately move on to the next item to maintain flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor group signals (volume and activity) as indicators of progress
rubrics_metrics.description: You can tell how a group is getting along by listening to the volume and looking at the general level of activity; these provide real-time feedback beyond individual utterances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use those macro-observations to adjust pace, introduce permission exercises, or step in with demonstration when the group collectively tightens or quiets.
